Question: What is happening to meat bones as they are being cooked for a stock?
Answer: What happens to bones simmering in water has a lot to do with collagen which are proteins in the structural portions of animal bodies. Collagen resides in the structural portions of an animal such as connective tissue, cartilage, bones, tendons, ligaments, and skin. So, bones are an important source of collagen. When collagen is hydrolyzed by cooking, it melts and forms gelatin. It is the amount of gelatin or hydrolyzed collagen that differentiates a broth from a stock. Cooking bones for a substantial amount of time melts collagen into gelatin, extracts and dissolves it the water, making stock. This adds a substantial amount of body and flavor to the water the bones are in which distinguishes it from broth. In my opinion, and in summary, water is okay to use in cooking, but broth is better, and rich stock is superior. Image Source: http://i.ytimg.com

Question: How do you not get annoyed when parents ask you random questions?
Answer: Congratulations. These days it seems nobody wants to get along and yet you are asking how to be less annoyed at your parents. Good for you. Learn this while you still have parents around. My advice is, don’t ignore their questions, answer, but be curious enough to ask your own questions and then listen. In my old age, I’m learning to ask questions and to be curious. It’s about time. I’m a story-telling kinda guy, but my wife is a questioner. For over 40 years, her questions have annoyed me. Then, I noticed that she would talk to others, on the phone for example, for long periods of time and direct the conversation by asking questions and then listening. She let others do the talking. You see, good questions draw people into better relationships. One day I was reading the Bible and I noticed that Jesus didn’t often answer questions directly. He seemed to prefer asking questions to answering them. He taught and told stories (parables for example), but he also asked a good deal of questions. The day I noticed, he had just been asked a trick question, and he said he would answer their question if they first answered one of his questions. He then asked a question that would reveal their true feelings, so they answered that they didn’t know the answer to his question. He didn’t answer their question, either. Now, you should answer your parents’s questions, but ask your own, too. Now, not all of my wife’s questions are good questions, some are asked out of habit, and your parents’s questions may not all be good ones, but yours can be.

Question: Why aren’t there any Apple or grape flavors of ice cream in ice cream parlors?
Answer: Apples are featured in ice creams, but not in overwhelming numbers, but grapes get a pass and for good reasons. In the ‘60s, Dutch Apple ice cream was a favorite flavor in Cabell’s ice cream for my family. Cabell’s was a Texas company that had a dairy line and over 60 convenience stores. Cabell’s was purchased by Southland Corp. in 1959 which owned 7-Eleven stores. As a kid in Texas, I worked at several Cabell’s Minit Markets and the ice cream line was excellent. Today, the Dutch Apple flavor can still be enjoyed but is rare, however, other apple flavored ice creams can be found such as apple pie, caramel apple, and apple swirl flavors. Now grapes have so much water, that they become little chunks of ice when frozen and just don’t lend themselves to making good ice cream (see Note). According to mashed.com, there's an urban legend that Ben Cohen (the front half of Ben & Jerry's) once made a batch of grape ice cream that killed Jerry's sister's dog, and swore off all further attempts. I don’t believe that, but I haven’t seen a grape flavored ice cream, either. NOTE: As pointed out in the comments, grapes have no more water than apples and other fruits found in ice cream). Also in comments, grape ice cream is made in Japan and other places.

Question: How do I freeze Roma tomatoes without peeling them?
Answer: We have a bumper crop of Roma’s right now for the number of plants we have and I’ll share my plans for freezing with you. If you don’t want to peel the tomatoes, you can wash and dry whole, crack-free, bug bite-free, Romas and freeze. People do this in so many ways, flash freezing (or not for smaller amounts), de-stemming (or not). The frozen tomatoes can be stored in zip-lock freezer bags, excluding air and labeled for use in cooking in a few months. To flash freeze, wash and dry ripe plum tomatoes place spaced apart on a parchment lined baking sheets. Place in the freezer for a couple of hours or longer to freeze. This assures the tomatoes don’t freeze in a large lump, but the shape of plum tomatoes especially with peels on, tend not to lump together much. While I have only blanched, quenched, slip-peeled and frozen tomatoes, there are many articles (often by homesteaders) online teaching that once thawed for a bit, the skins slip right off and can be further thawed, cut and cooked as you need. Some folks wash, dry, de-stem and quarter plum tomatoes with their skins on. Once drained on kitchen paper and flash frozen, these can be bagged without sticking together. Keep in mind that freezing changes the texture so that using in salads is not as likely as using in cooking.

Question: Why is potato bread the most delicious bread?

Softness: Breads react well to changes in the starches they are made with. Potato starch adds a softness and fluffiness to breads as it extends shelf life, especially with added enrichments like fats or dairy. Asian breads like Tangzhong breads (water roux or yu-dane) are not made with potatoes, but are fluffy and long-lived as well, and that may be because a portion of the wheat starch in the flour is gelled before the bread is made. Donuts: As a side note, the first chain of donut shops in the US was Spudnuts, which were very popular in the ’50s and ’60s. Question: How does the thickness of aluminum foil affect its ability to retain heat when used for cooking or wrapping food?
Answer: Covering is more important for retaining heat than what is used. As long as the foil covering is compatible with the food and continuous, its thickness isn’t that important. In other words, in cooking, I don’t think heat loss (or gain) by conduction is as strong a factor as is trapping steam, radiation, and convection are. How the foil holds up is important and thickness plays a role, however, in cooking and in freezing foods. As a old engineer, I’ve forgotten most of my heat transfer stuff but I do remember sizing heating systems for tanks of all sizes. The vast majority of the heat loss was almost always from the surface. Any effective cover, even ping-pong balls floating on top, worked to keep heat in. With cooking, a cover reduces heat loss from evaporation primarily and pots heat up more quickly and covered baking items tend to steam-cook or braise. Foil also controls browning from radiated heat regardless of its thickness. With freezing, it’s all about sealing the food and keeping air out. Thickness is important here as thin foil tends to tear in the freezer. That would be “tearible.”
